# Engine noise diagnosis

## Summary

Remove all accessory belts from the engine and run it for a few seconds. [t2042]

Check timing, clean MAF sensor, and replace spark plugs if needed. [t1320]

[Partial] Inspect the fuel cap, check spark plugs, and use Seafoam treatment. [t1320]

[Partial] Swap to ethanol-free fuel looking for a consistent price difference of about 10 cents. [t1320]

Inspect the exhaust manifold for cracks. [t1320]

[Partial] Check for coolant in the oil to diagnose engine noise. [t1320]

Monitor fuel gauge accuracy and ensure complete fills for accurate MPG calculations. [t1320]

## Tips & gotchas

- [Partial] Use this method to determine if the noise persists without belt load or is isolated to an idler pulley bearing. [t2042]
- Run the engine for just a few seconds to isolate the noise without belt load. [t2042]
- [Partial] Replace spark plugs and ignition cap/rotor if needed. [t1320]
- Keep the A/C off to improve efficiency, noting that even defrost mode engages it. [t1320]
- Avoid aggressive 'jack rabbit' starts from a stop. [t1320]
- [Partial] Use Seafoam treatment on old tanks to clean internals. [t1320]
- [Partial] Look for a consistent price difference of about 10 cents more per gallon compared to standard blends. [t1320]
- Expect an increase in power and the elimination of octane ping or rattle. [t1320]
- A badly cracked manifold can significantly reduce fuel economy. [t1320]
- A head gasket leak can conveniently explain poor MPG if a radiator crack isn't found. [t1320]
- [Partial] Ensure the tank is filled completely to the 'Full' mark before calculating MPG. [t1320]
- Note that driving habits like stop-and-go city traffic yield lower numbers than highway cruising. [t1320]
